## Slide 1 — Title & One-Line Problem

**Purpose:** Establish who is presenting, under what supervision, on what stream, and state the problem in one sentence precise enough that the panel doesn't need slide 2 to know what's at stake.

**On-slide content:**
- Title: **A Self-Healing Multi-Agent System for Semantic Error Diagnosis, Verified Repair and Recovery** — short title **Granite**
- Project code: **F26-060-Granite**
- Team: Shahoud Shahid (23i-2515) · Muhammad Noor (23i-2520) · Saif Shahzad (23i-2634)
- Supervisor: **Dr. Adil Majeed**
- Stream: **A — Research-derived**
- One-line problem: *"When a multi-agent AI system fails — including when the wrong answer looks completely right — no published method can reliably say which agent caused it, and none can verify a fix before trusting it."*

**Visual:** Dark title slide (graphite ground, gold accent). No diagram — the sentence carries the slide.

**Evidence/Source:** `FYP_Registration_Form_Answers.md` (title decision record); `Proposal_Defense_Package.md` slide 1.

**Presenter emphasis:**
- Say the one-line problem exactly as written — it's built to name WHO (teams running multi-agent systems), WHAT fails (attribution + silent failures), WHY it matters (nobody can verify a fix) in one breath.
- Do not explain the title word-by-word — slide 6 does that.

## Slide 2 — Stakeholders, Problem & Current Workflow

**Purpose:** Establish that the problem is real, who has it, and exactly where today's workflow breaks down — before any solution is proposed.

**On-slide content:**
- **Primary stakeholder:** an engineering team operating a multi-agent AI system in or near production — grounded concretely in a customer-support/retail workflow (the active benchmark substrate, tau-bench retail)
- **Secondary stakeholders:** downstream product teams who consume the diagnosis output; auditors/compliance reviewers who need traceable evidence of what went wrong
- **Current workflow:** an observability platform (LangSmith / Langfuse / Braintrust / Arize) captures the execution trace → a human reads it and guesses the root cause
- **Where it fails:** no automated attribution with published accuracy; no systematic check for *silent failures* (a confident, well-formed, wrong answer with no error signal); no way to test a candidate fix before redeploying it
- **Consequence:** a missed silent failure ships an incorrect answer to an end user, undetected
- **SDG:** SDG 9 — Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure (target 9.5)

**Visual:** 3-step process strip — *Capture trace → Human reads → Guesses root cause* — with a red "unmeasured" tag on the third step, retitled "now measured" once the 06 doc's human-baseline study runs (FYP-2).

**Evidence/Source:** `FYP_Scope_CCP_and_Implementation_Plan.md` §0.05–§0.06; Who&When's own reported baseline (single-LLM guess: **14.2% step accuracy** — the empirical cost of "just reading the trace").

**Presenter emphasis:**
- The stakeholder line is what turns CCP characteristic #6 from weak to clear — name who was actually contacted, or say plainly that this is still in progress and name the date it closes.
- 14.2% is not our number — it's the field's own measured baseline for "a human/single model reads the trace." It's the number the whole project is trying to beat.

## Slide 4 — Research & Technical Basis

**Purpose:** Show the literature was read for decisions, not decoration.

**On-slide content:**
- Lineage: **Who&When** (ICML 2025, 14.2%) → **AgenTracer** (ICLR 2026, fault-injection methodology) → **SDBL, TraceElephant, ErrorProbe** (ACL 2026 Findings, 59.5% SOTA) → **AgentAsk, PROTEA** (ACL 2026 Demo)
- **ErrorProbe chosen as baseline** — on performance, not recency (beats its ancestors on their own benchmarks)
- **CrewAI + LangGraph chosen as committed frameworks** — neither used by any of the 9 papers reviewed, which is the actual test of generalization
- **Constraint-based (not LLM-judge) silent-failure detection chosen** because the literature shows LLM judges perform poorly here — "From Confident Closing to Silent Failure" (arXiv:2606.09863) reports LLM-judge AUROC ≤0.65 on tau2-bench/AppWorld
- **Single-framework scope-narrowing rejected** — the market survey's own advice, explicitly declined because it would delete the cross-architecture research question (risk-register R19)

**Visual:** lineage/accuracy ladder — three bars rising to 59.5%, with a shaded "40.5% still wrong" cap.

**Evidence/Source:** `Full_Literature_Landscape_Analysis.md`; `ErrorProbe_Baseline_Selection.md`; risk-register R7 (literature triage), R19.

**Presenter emphasis:**
- State the backbone-confound caveat before being asked: cross-paper comparisons use different LLM backbones, so a win partly reflects backbone strength — controlled for within Granite's own experiments.
- Name that unpublished, credible preprints exist in adjacent territory (DoVer, the silent-failure detection paper) and that the team made a recorded decision not to chase every one — the strategy is beating a peer-reviewed baseline, not pre-empting unpublished work.

## Slide 6 — Proposed Solution & Contribution

**Purpose:** State exactly what's being built and why the combination is the contribution.

**On-slide content:**
- **Contribution statement:** *Existing failure-attribution methods (Who&When, AgenTracer, SDBL, ErrorProbe) reach up to 59.5% step accuracy but remain weak under two conditions: none is evaluated on an architecture absent from its own benchmark construction, and the strongest method admits it cannot catch silent failures. We are building a cross-architecture fault-injection benchmark and a diagnosis pipeline with constraint-based silent-failure verification, packaged as a framework-agnostic testing SDK.*
- **Pipeline, one line:** trace → execution graph → Semantic Error Diagnostic (parallel, unconditional) → backward causal trace → Repair Agent → controlled counterfactual replay → confidence-gated recommendation
- **In scope:** the 10 committed mechanisms (see slide 9) · **Out of scope:** message queues, Kubernetes/multi-region, full RBAC, disaster-recovery infrastructure, multi-tenant billing (SDS §1)
- **Deployment target:** single Docker container, cloud VM or on-prem

**Visual:** Architecture diagram — 3 owner lanes (Data/Benchmark, Diagnosis, Platform) inside one system boundary, operator and target system outside it, one external LLM API box. (Full detailed version: Granite Architecture Atlas, Diagram 1.)

**Evidence/Source:** `FYP_Scope_CCP_and_Implementation_Plan.md` §3, §6; `Software_Design_Specification.md` §3–4.

**Presenter emphasis:**
- Say unprompted: "controlled, not deterministic" — the replay protocol is deterministic, LLM-step variance is measured over N replays, never assumed away (R25).
- Say unprompted: the Semantic Error Diagnostic is scoped to task specs with machine-checkable constraints and abstains elsewhere, with the abstention rate reported as a metric — not a claim to detect arbitrary wrongness.

## Slide 7 — POC / Feasibility Evidence (mandatory)

**Purpose:** Show evidence, not describe that evidence exists — per the handbook's own words, "a POC that disproved the assumption is usually more valuable."

**On-slide content — 8 real spikes, each labeled by status:**

| Spike | Status | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 — ErrorProbe reproduction (simplified) | **Demonstrated** | agent accuracy 62.5–85.7% (mean 71.4%), step accuracy 0–25% (mean 13.2%) — 8 cases × 5 real runs, range reported not a point estimate |
| 2 — CrewAI instrumentation | **Demonstrated** | Clean trace: 3 nodes, 2 correctly-ordered edges |
| 3 / 3b — Fault injection | **Demonstrated** | Ground truth recoverable and unambiguous; one case self-corrected by the agent — kept as a finding |
| 4 — Semantic Error Diagnostic | **Demonstrated** | Catches known-wrong values incl. a plausible near-miss ($20.00 vs. $19.75 true), zero false positives |
| 5 — Controlled counterfactual replay | **Demonstrated** | Corrupted trace 97.2 → recovered 108.0, `recovery_success: true` |
| 6 — Cyclic graph handling | **Demonstrated** | True cycle terminates correctly; control run with the bound disabled hit the 10,000-step safety cap — proves the bound is load-bearing |
| 7 — Preventive classifier | **Demonstrated — honest negative** | precision/recall/F1 = **0.25**, near-random on hand-written data — real finding, not hidden |
| 8 — Repair Agent | **Demonstrated** | repair_success_rate **4/6 (0.667)**; both failures share one precisely diagnosed, fixable interface cause |

**Full reproduction (comparable-class backbone) — Currently in progress**, top FYP-1 priority. **Tier 2 gates (Recovery Controller, Verified Repair Memory) — Planned**, pre-registered Mid-1 decision criteria, not yet run.

**Visual:** the real JSON outputs / the live `poc-demo` console screenshot showing Spike 1's multi-run range and Spike 8's real repair pair — "shown, not described."

**Evidence/Source:** `POC_Spike_Outputs_Full.md`; `dev/spikes/poc/*.json`; `poc-demo/` (live console reading the same real files).

**Presenter emphasis:**
- Lead with Spike 7's negative result and Spike 8's failure analysis — the guide's own words on this are worth quoting directly.
- Every number on this slide is real, computed from files in this repo — say that once, plainly, and move on.

## Slide 8 — Evaluation Plan

**Purpose:** Define exactly how success is measured, with thresholds decided before any result exists.

**On-slide content:**
- **Baseline:** ErrorProbe, reproduced — **pre-registered acceptance band: ±10 points of the published 59.5%** on a comparable-class backbone (Sonnet 5); outside the band, both numbers reported transparently (Annex A.2)
- **Data:** Who&When (184 real cases, in hand) + new cross-architecture benchmark (floor 500 / stretch 1,000 traces, **15–20% deliberately clean controls**)
- **Metrics:** agent/step accuracy · propagation-path F1 · silent-failure precision/recall + **coverage (abstention rate)** · **pipeline false-positive rate on clean controls** · task completion rate · recovery rate · repair success rate · **false repair rate** · **diagnostic latency overhead (measurable NFR, target &lt;50%)**
- **Statistical protocol:** bootstrap 95% CIs, fixed seeds, N=5 replay variance, 4-item pre-declared ablation matrix, human-baseline comparison
- **Success bands:** *failure* = no measurable improvement anywhere · *acceptable* = parity on Who&When + any cross-arch result + nonzero-coverage silent-failure detection · *strong* = beats baseline on unseen architectures, &gt;70% silent-failure recall · *exceptional* = strong + &gt;50% verified-repair recovery at low false-repair rate
- **What this evidence cannot support:** production-scale reliability claims beyond the tested frameworks and domains — stated up front, not extracted under questioning

**Visual:** metrics-to-claims map — each research question paired with the metric that answers it.

**Evidence/Source:** `FYP_Scope_CCP_and_Implementation_Plan.md` §11; `06_Expanded_Scope_and_Feasibility_Plan.md` §3.1–3.2.

**Presenter emphasis:**
- The false-positive-rate-on-clean-controls metric is absent from every paper in the reviewed corpus and every commercial platform checked — say this is the one metric the whole field is missing, not just us.
- The acceptance band was declared **before** the full reproduction runs — that ordering is the point, not a footnote.

## Slide 9 — Scope, Risks & Dependencies

**Purpose:** Separate what's promised from what's possible, and show every major risk already has a stated fallback.

**On-slide content:**
- **Committed core — 10 items, two evidence tiers:** Tier 1 (8, each with a real spike): fault-injection harness, cross-architecture benchmark, Culprit Agent, Error Step Localization, Verification Agent, Semantic Error Diagnostic, Repair Agent, Verified Automatic Repair. Tier 2 (2, gated, pre-registered Mid-1 criteria): Recovery Controller (no POC yet), Verified Repair Memory (one real test, failed — 0/8, stated honestly)
- **8 extensions, gated behind the core** — built only after it works
- **Resources:** **$0, committed for the full project** — local Ollama throughout, including the reproduction and evaluation (R37, 2026-09-04). The paid-tier alternative was priced from measured token counts and explicitly rejected: ≈$353 recommended / ≈$881 pessimistic ceiling for a comparable-class backbone. Accepted tradeoff: the reproduction is now expected to fall outside the ±10-point acceptance band on backbone strength alone, reported via Annex A.2 dual-reporting
- **Tools/stack:** Python, FastAPI, React/TypeScript, Postgres, Docker, CrewAI, LangGraph, Ollama, GitHub Actions
- **Top risks + fallback:**

| Risk | Fallback |
|---|---|
| Reproduction misses the ±10pt band (R1) | Transparent dual-reporting, Annex A.2 |
| Recovery Controller gate fails (R21) | Resume via controlled replay — Tier 1 already delivers it |
| Verified Repair Memory re-test fails again (R22) | Ships as a memory-on/off ablation — a legitimate evaluation contribution |
| Benchmark scale stalls | Floor of 500, or 300-with-full-statistics beats 1,000-without |
| LLM API unavailable at runtime | Documented degraded state, not a crash (plan §13) |

- **Ethical/professional:** advisory-only diagnosis, human-gated fix approval; informed consent required for any real user's trace data; synthetic fault injection restricted to own/consenting systems only

**Visual:** two-tier core diagram with gate icons on Tier 2; four-band scope funnel (Core/Advanced/Stretch/Future).

**Evidence/Source:** `FYP_Scope_CCP_and_Implementation_Plan.md` §7.0, §7.2; `cost-estimate.md`; `risk-register.md`.

**Presenter emphasis:**
- Deliver this slide as confidence, not confession: decision rules were pre-registered before results exist, which is exactly what the guide's change-control section (§5.3) asks for.
- If feasibility is pressed: point at the effort-budget number on slide 10, don't just reassure verbally.

## Final Recommended Slide Order

**No rearrangement from the 10-slide structure above.** It already follows the defense-oriented narrative the brief asks for (problem → users → gap → research → complexity → solution → feasibility → proof plan → scope discipline → people), and it is the same order the handbook's own C.16 names and the order already rehearsed in `Proposal_Defense_Package.md`. Changing it now would cost rehearsal continuity for no narrative gain.

## Overall Narrative

Slides 1–2 establish the problem is real and who has it. Slides 3–4 prove the gap is structural (not a missing feature) and that the literature was read for decisions, not decoration. Slide 5 earns capstone status with evidence per Seoul Accord characteristic. Slide 6 states what's actually being built and draws the scope boundary. Slide 7 is the pivot of the whole deck — real evidence, including two honest negative results, that the riskiest assumptions have already been tested. Slide 8 shows the team knows how it will judge its own success before the data exists. Slide 9 shows the scope is bounded and every major risk has a fallback already written down. Slide 10 closes on people, timeline, and the compliance lines the handbook names explicitly. The throughline across all ten: every claim is followed immediately by the evidence for it, never left to stand alone.

## Panel Attack Points

*Condensed from `02_Panel_Defense_Question_Bank.md` Part A — the ten questions built specifically to end a defense, each with the answer already rehearsed.*

| # | Attack | Required evidence / answer |
|---|---|---|
| A1 | "Your title says *Self-Healing... Verified Repair and Recovery* — one of those has never been built, the other failed its only test." | 8/10 core items evidenced; Tier 2's two weakest items carry pre-registered Mid-1 gates with recorded fallbacks — lead with this, don't wait to be asked |
| A2 | "This is three projects — reproduction, benchmark, product — for three people in one year." | One pipeline, not three; ~1,130-hour budget summing inside capacity, named per line, walking skeleton retiring integration risk at Mid-1 not Final-1 |
| A3 | "Your reproduction averages 13% step accuracy vs. ErrorProbe's 59.5%." | Deliberately simplified spike (no tool-grounding, no memory), 5-run range reported honestly; full reproduction scheduled with a pre-registered ±10pt band and a transparent-reporting fallback |
| A4 | "Why isn't this just ChatGPT?" | Fault-injection harness makes accuracy measurable, not a vibe; 0%-API silent-failure check catches what a chat can't be asked to catch; 80–85% of components never call a model |
| A5 | "LangSmith/Arize already shipped this, with more engineers." | Checked directly, positioning corrected on the record (R9); neither confirms published step-level accuracy, general silent-failure detection, or measured counterfactual recovery |
| A6 | "Rules can't understand meaning — your SED claim is either trivial or impossible." | Scoped explicitly to machine-checkable constraints, abstains elsewhere, abstention rate reported as a metric |
| A7 | "You claim deterministic re-execution of LLM calls — LLMs aren't deterministic." | Corrected wording: the protocol is deterministic, LLM-step variance is measured over N replays, never assumed away (R25) |
| A8 | "This design came from a market-survey document — whose project is this?" | Survey was one input among nine papers and seven platforms; its central scope advice (single-framework) was explicitly rejected (R19), on the record |
| A9 | "You're grading yourself on a benchmark you built." | Ground-truth-by-construction is the field's own established method (AgenTracer/TracerTraj); realism comes from the unmodified task substrates (tau-bench, GSM8K) |
| A10 | "Couldn't AI build this whole system in two weeks?" | Names precisely what a generated version gets wrong: cross-framework instrumentation, the benchmark's validation labor, faithful reproduction fidelity, and every measured trade-off in the evaluation |
